readings.c3s3:
¶
'''whip-crane''' (hwip′krān), ''n.'' A simple and rapid-working form of crane, used in unloading vessels. ''E. H. Knight.''

'''whip-crop''' (hwip′krop), ''n.'' A name given to the whitebeam (''Pyrus Aria''), to the wayfaring-tree (''Viburnum Lantana''), and to the guelder-rose (''V. Opulus''), from the use of their stems for whip-stocks. ''Britten and Holland.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''whip-fish''' (hwip′fish), ''n.'' A chætodont fish, ''Heniochus macrolepidotus'', having one of the spines of the dorsal fin produced into a long filament like a whip-lash.

'''whip-gin''' (hwip′jin), ''n.'' A simple tackle-block with a hoisting-rope running over it: same as ''gin-block''.

'''whip-graft''' (hwip′gräft), ''v. t.'' To graft by cutting the scion and stock in a sloping direction, so as to fit each other, and by inserting a tongue on the scion into a slit in the stock.

'''whip-grass''' (hwip′gräs), ''n.'' An American species of nut-grass, ''Scleria triglomerata''.

'''whip-hand''' (hwip′hand), ''n.'' '''1.''' The hand that holds the whip in riding or driving—that is, the right hand.
{{smaller block|Mr. Tulliver was a peremptory man, and, as he said, would never let anybody get hold of his ''whip-hand''.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Mill on the Floss, i. 5.}}}}
'''2.''' An advantage, or advantageous position.
{{smaller block|The archangel . . . has the ''whip-hand'' of her. ''Dryden.''

Now, what say you, Mr. Flamefire? I shall have the ''whiphand'' of you presently. {{right|''Vanbrugh'', Æsop, v. 1.}}}}

'''whiphandle''' (hwip′han″dl), ''n.'' '''1.''' The handle of a whip. See ''whip-hand'', 2, and compare ''whip-row''.—'''2†.''' See the quotation.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|whip|6902|whiphandle}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''2.''' To overlay, as a cord, rope, etc., with a cord, twine, or thread going round and round it; inwrap; seize; serve with twine, thread, or the like wound closely and tightly round and round: generally with ''about'', ''around'', ''over'', etc.

{{smaller block|''Whipped over'' either with gold thread, silver, or silk.
{{right|''Stubbes.'' (''Imp. Dict.'')}}}}

{{smaller block|The same stringes, beeing by the Archers themselves with fine threed well ''whipt'', did also verie seldom breake.
{{right|''Sir J. Smyth'', Discourses on Weapons, etc., quoted in [Ellis’s Lit. Letters, p. 54.}}}}

{{smaller block|Its string is firmly ''whipped about'' with small gut.
{{right|''Moxon'', Mechanical Exercises.}}}}

'''3.''' To lay regularly on; serve in regular circles round and round.

{{smaller block|''Whip'' your silk twice or thrice about the root-end of the feather, hook, and towght.
{{right|''Cotton'', in Walton’s Angler, ii. 245.}}}}

'''4.''' To sew with an over and over stitch, as two pieces of cloth whose edges are laid or stitched together; overcast: as, to ''whip'' a seam.—'''5.''' To gather by a kind of combination running and overhand stitch: as, to ''whip'' a ruffle.

<poem>In half-''whipt'' muslin needles useless lie,
And shuttle-cocks across the counter fly.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Gay'', Trivia, ii. 339.}}}}

'''6.''' ''Naut.'', to hoist or purchase by means of a rope passed through a single pulley.—'''7.''' To strike with a whip or lash, or with anything tough and flexible; lash; use a whip upon: as, to ''whip'' a horse.

{{smaller block|At night, the lights put out and company removed, they ''whipped'' themselves in their Chappell on Mount Calvary. {{right|''Sandys'', Travailes, p. 132.}}}}
{{smaller block|It blew so violently before they recovered the House that the Boughs of the Trees ''whipt'' them sufficiently before they got thither; and it rained as hard as before.
{{right|''Dampier'', Voyages, II. iii. 69.}}}}
'''8.''' To punish with a whip, scourge, birch, or the like; flog: as, to ''whip'' a vagrant; to ''whip'' a perverse boy.
{{smaller block|Fough! body of Jove! I’ll have the slave ''whipt'' one of these days.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Poetaster, iv. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|A country scholler in England should be ''whipped'' for speaking the like.
{{right|''Coryat'', Crudities, I. 20.}}}}
{{smaller block|I was never carted but in harvest; never ''whipt'' but at school.
{{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, i. 3.}}}}
'''9.''' To outdo; overcome; beat: as, to ''whip'' creation. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|A man without a particle of Greek ''whipped'' (to speak Kentuckicé) whole crowds of sleeping drones who had more than they could turn to any good account.
{{right|''De Quincey'', Herodotus.}}}}
'''10.''' To drive with lashes.
{{smaller block|<poem>Consideration, like an angel, came,
And ''whipp’d'' the offending Adam out of him.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., i. 1. 29.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>This said, the scourge his forward horses drave
Through ev’ry order; and, with him, all ''whipp’d'' their chariots on,
All threat’ningly, out-thund’ring shouts as earth were overthrown.</poem>
{{right|''Chapman'', Iliad, xv. 319.}}}}
'''11.''' To lash, in a figurative sense; treat with cutting severity, as with sarcasm or abuse.
{{smaller block|Wilt thou ''whip'' thine own faults in other men?
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of A., v. 1. 40.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I look’d and read, and saw how finely Wit
Had ''whipp’d'' itself; and then grew friends with it.</poem>
{{right|''J. Beaumont'', Psyche, ii. 62.}}}} '''12.''' To cause to spin or rotate by lashing with a whip or scourge-stick: said of a top.
{{smaller block|Since I plucked geese, played truant and ''whipped'' top.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., v. 1. 27.}}}}
{{smaller block|He was ''whipt'' like a top.
{{right|''Fletcher'', Loyal Subject, v. 4.}}}}
'''13.''' To thrash; beat out, as grain by striking: as, to ''whip'' wheat. ''Imp. Dict.''—'''14.''' To beat into a froth, as eggs, cream, etc., with a whisk, fork, spoon, or other implement.
{{smaller block|To make Clouted cream and ''whipt'' Sillabubs?
{{right|''Shadwell'', The Scowrers.}}}}
'''15.''' To fish upon with a fly or other bait; draw a fly or other bait along the surface of: as, to ''whip'' a stream.
{{smaller block|He shot with the pistol, he fenced, he ''whipped'' the trout-stream, . . . but somehow everything went amiss with him. {{right|''Lever'', Davenport Dunn, xxiii.}}}}
'''16.''' To bring or keep together as a party whip does: as, to ''whip'' a party into line. See ''whip'', ''n.'', 3 (''b'').
{{smaller block|Lord Essex was there, . . . ''whipping'' up for a dinner-party, cursing and swearing at all his friends for being out of town. {{right|''Macaulay'', in Trevelyan, I. v.}}}}
{{smaller block|The only bond of cohesion is the caucus, which occasionally ''whips'' a party together for cooperative action against the time for casting its vote upon some critical question. {{right|''W. Wilson'', Cong. Gov., ii.}}}}

{{smaller|'''To whip in''', to keep from scattering, as hounds in a hunt; hence, to bring or keep (the members of a party) together, as in a legislative assembly.—'''To whip off''', to drive (hounds) off a scent.}}

{{smaller block|The difficult nature of the covert, and the fact that they were running in view, prevented hounds being ''whipped off'' at the outset.{{right|''The Field'', April 4, 1885. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}}

'''To whip the cat.''' {{smaller|(''a'') To practise the most pinching parsimony. ''Forby.'' [Prov. Eng.] (''b'') To go from house to house to work, as a tailor or other workman. Compare ''whip-cat.'' [Scotch and prov. Eng. and U. S.]}}

{{smaller block|Mr. Hart . . . made shoes, a trade he prosecuted in an itinerating manner from house to house, ''whipping the cat'', as it was termed.{{right|''S. Judd'', Margaret, i. 3.}}}}

{{smaller|(''c''†) To get tipsy. ''Halliwell.''}}—'''To whip the devil around the stump.''' {{smaller|See ''devil.''}}

'''whip''' (hwip), ''n.''   [< ME. ''whippe'', ''quippe'' = MD. ''wippe'', a whip, D. ''wip'', a swipe, strappado, moment: see ''whip'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' An instrument for flagellation, whether in driving animals or in punishing human beings; a scourge. {{smaller|In its typical form it is composed of a lash of some kind fastened upon a handle more or less rigid; the common form of horsewhip has little or no lash, being a long, tapering, and very pliant switch-like rod of wood, whalebone, or other material, usually wound or braided over with thread.}}

{{smaller block|And alle the folk of the Contree ryden comounly with outen Spores: but thei beren alle weys a lytille ''Whippe'' in hire Hondes, for to chacen with hire Hors.{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 249.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The dwarf . . .
Struck at him with his ''whip'', and cut his cheek.</poem>{{right|''Tennyson'', Geraint.}}}}

'''2.''' One who handles a whip, as in driving a coach or carriage; a driver: as, an expert ''whip.''

{{smaller block|What the devil do you do with a wig, Thomas?—none of the London ''whips'' of any degree of ton wear wigs now.{{right|''Sheridan'', The Rivals, i. 1.}}}}

{{smaller block|That is the famous coaching baronet, than whom no better ''whip'' has ever been seen upon the road.
{{right|''W. Besant'', Fifty Years Ago, p. 50.}}}}
'''3.''' A whipper-in. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') In ''hunting'', the person who manages the hounds.}}
{{smaller block|After these the body of the pack—the parson of the parish, and a hard-riding cornet at home on leave; then the huntsman, the first ''whip'', nearly a quorum of magistrates, etc.
{{right|''Whyte Melville'', White Rose, II. xv.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') In English parliamentary usage, a member who performs certain non-official but important duties in looking after the interests of his party, especially the securing of the attendance of as many members as possible at important divisions: as, the Liberal ''whip''; the Conservative ''whip''. See the quotation.}}
{{smaller block|The ''whip’s'' duties are (1) to inform every member belonging to the party when an important division may be expected, and, if he sees the member in or about the House, to keep him there until the division is called; (2) to direct the members of his own party how to vote; (3) to obtain pairs for them if they cannot be present to vote; (4) to “tell,” i. e., count the members in every party division; (5) to “keep touch” of opinion within the party, and convey to the leader a faithful impression of that opinion, from which the latter can judge how far he may count on the support of his whole party in any course he proposes to take.
{{right|''J. Bryce'', American Commonwealth, I. 199.}}}}
'''4.''' A call made upon the members of a party to be in their places at a certain time: as, both parties have issued a rigorous ''whip'' in view of the expected division. [Eng.]—'''5.''' A contrivance for hoisting, consisting of a rope and pulley and usually a snatch-block, and worked by one or more horses which in hoisting walk away from the thing hoisted. In mining usually called ''whip-and-derry''. See cut under ''cable-laid''.—'''6.''' One of the radii or arms of a windmill, to which the sails are attached; also, the length of the arm reckoned from the shaft.
{{smaller block|The arm, or ''whip'', of one of the sails.
{{right|''Rankine'', Steam Engine, § 188.}}}}
'''7.''' In ''angling'', the leader of an angler’s cast with its flies attached. {{smaller|The fly at the end is the drag-fly, tail-fly, or stretcher; those above are the drop-flies, droppers, or bobbers. More fully called a ''whip of flies.''}} '''8.''' A vibrating spring used as an electric circuit-closer for testing capacity. {{smaller|The spring is permanently connected to one plate of the condenser or cable, and vibrates between two studs, contact with one of which closes a battery circuit, and with the other a galvanometer circuit. The condenser is thus in rapid succession charged from the battery and discharged through the galvanometer. The indications of the latter are thus proportional to the rate of vibration and the capacity of the condenser.}} '''9.''' A slender rod or flexible pole used instead of stakes to mark the bounds of oyster-beds.—'''10.''' The common black swift, ''Cypselus apus''. [Prov. Eng.]—'''11.''' A preparation of cream, eggs, etc., beaten to a froth.
{{smaller block|There were “''whips''” and “floating-islands” and jellies to compound. {{right|''The Century'', XXXVII. 841.}}}}
'''Crack-the-whip.''' {{smaller|Same as ''snap-the-whip''.}}—'''Six-stringed whip''', {{smaller|or}} '''the whip with six strings''', {{smaller|the Six Articles. See ''article''.}}—'''Snap-the-whip''', {{smaller|a game played in running or skating. A number of persons join hands and move rapidly forward in line; those at one end stop suddenly and swing the rest sharply around; the contest is to see whether any of the outer part of the line can thus be thrown down or made to break their hold. Also called ''crack-the-whip''.}}—'''To drink''' {{smaller|or}} '''lick on (upon) the whip†''', {{smaller|to have a taste of the whip; get a thrashing.}}
<poem>In fayth and for youre long taryng
Ye shal ''lik on the whyp.''</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Towneley Mysteries'', p. 30.}}}}
<poem>Comes naked neede? and chance to do amisse?
He shal be sure, to ''drinke vpon the whippe.''</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Gascoigne'', Steele Glas (ed. Arber, p. 68).}}}}

'''Whip and spur''', making use of both whip and spur in riding; hence, with the utmost haste.

{{smaller block|Came ''whip and spur'', and dash’d through thick and thin.
{{right|''Pope'', Dunciad, iv. 197.}}}}

'''whip''' (hwip), ''adv.''   [An elliptical use of ''whip'', ''v.'' Cf. LG. ''wips!'' quickly, = Sw. Dan. ''vips!'' pop! quick!]   With a sudden change; at once; quick.

{{smaller block|You are no sooner chose in but ''whip!'' you are as proud as the devil. {{right|''Mrs. Centlivre'', Gotham Election, i. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|When I came, ''whip'' was the key turned upon the girls.
{{right|''Richardson'', Clarissa Harlowe, VIII. 267. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''whip-and-derry''' (hwip′a̤nd-der′i), ''n.'' The simplest form of machinery, with the exception of the windlass, for hoisting. {{smaller|It consists of a rope passing over a pulley, and is worked by a horse or horses. It is rarely used in mining, except in very shallow mines. Sometimes called simply ''whip'', and sometimes ''whipsey-derry''.}}

'''whipcan†''' (hwip′kan), ''n.''   [< ''whip'', ''v.'', + obj. ''can''<sup>2</sup>.]   A hard drinker.

{{smaller block|He would prove an especial good fellow, and singular ''whip-can.'' {{right|''Urquhart'', tr. of Rabelais, i. 8. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''whipcat''' (hwip′kat), ''n.'' and ''a.''   [< ''whip'', ''v.'', + obj. ''cat.'']   '''I.''' ''n.'' A tailor or other workman who “whips the cat.” See ''to whip the cat'' (''b''), under ''whip''. [Colloq.]

{{smaller block|A tailor who “whipped the cat” (or went out to work at his customers’ houses) would occupy a day, at easy labour, at a cost of 1s. 6d. (or less) in money, and the ''whipcat’s'' meals . . . included.
{{right|''Mayhew'', London Labour and London Poor, II. 414.}}}}
'''II.†''' ''a.'' Drunken.
{{smaller block|With ''whip-cat'' bowling they kept a myrry carousing.
{{right|''Stanihurst'', Æneid, iii.}}}}

'''whip-cord''' (hwip′kôrd), ''n.'' '''1.''' A strong twisted hempen cord, so called because lashes or snappers of whips are made from it.
{{smaller block|Let ’s step into this shop, and buy a pennyworth of ''whip-cord'' . . . to spin my top.
{{right|''Kingsley'', Westward Ho, iii.}}}}
'''2.''' A cord or string of catgut.
{{smaller block|In order to produce a cord — known as ''whipcord'' — from these intestines, they are sewn together by means of the filandre before mentioned, the joints being cut aslant to make them smoother and stronger.
{{right|''Spons’ Encyc. Manuf.'', I. 609.}}}}
'''3.''' A seaweed, ''Chorda filum'', having a very long, slender, whip-like frond. See ''Chorda'', 2. {{smaller|—'''Whip-cord couching''', embroidery in which a heavy whip-cord is laid upon the material and is covered by the silk couching, which is afterward sewed closely down upon the background on each side of the whip-cord, so as to leave a decided ridge.—'''Whip-cord willow.''' See ''willow''.}}

'''whip-cordy''' (hwip′kôr″di), ''a.''   [< ''whip-cord'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   Like whip-cord; sinewy; muscular. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The bishop [of Exeter was] wonderfully hale and ''whip-cordy''.
{{right|''Bp. Wilberforce'', in Life, II. 336. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}}

'''whip-crane''' (hwip′krān), ''n.'' A simple and rapid-working form of crane, used in unloading vessels. ''E. H. Knight.''

'''whip-crop''' (hwip′krop), ''n.'' A name given to the whitebeam (''Pyrus Aria''), to the wayfaring-tree (''Viburnum Lantana''), and to the guelder-rose (''V. Opulus''), from the use of their stems for whip-stocks. ''Britten and Holland.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''whip-fish''' (hwip′fish), ''n.'' A chætodont fish, ''Heniochus macrolepidotus'', having one of the spines of the dorsal fin produced into a long filament like a whip-lash.

'''whip-gin''' (hwip′jin), ''n.'' A simple tackle-block with a hoisting-rope running over it: same as ''gin-block''.

'''whip-graft''' (hwip′gräft), ''v. t.'' To graft by cutting the scion and stock in a sloping direction, so as to fit each other, and by inserting a tongue on the scion into a slit in the stock.

'''whip-grass''' (hwip′gräs), ''n.'' An American species of nut-grass, ''Scleria triglomerata''.

'''whip-hand''' (hwip′hand), ''n.'' '''1.''' The hand that holds the whip in riding or driving—that is, the right hand.
{{smaller block|Mr. Tulliver was a peremptory man, and, as he said, would never let anybody get hold of his ''whip-hand''.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Mill on the Floss, i. 5.}}}}
'''2.''' An advantage, or advantageous position.
{{smaller block|The archangel . . . has the ''whip-hand'' of her. ''Dryden.''

Now, what say you, Mr. Flamefire? I shall have the ''whiphand'' of you presently. {{right|''Vanbrugh'', Æsop, v. 1.}}}}

'''whiphandle''' (hwip′han″dl), ''n.'' '''1.''' The handle of a whip. See ''whip-hand'', 2, and compare ''whip-row''.—'''2†.''' See the quotation.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
